name: PT Janu Putra Sejahtera Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Janu Putra Sejahtera: a poultry recovery that belongs to the asset buyer, not the shareholder
frontmatter.summary: AYAM's profit is carried by other income the interim accounts do not decompose, not by the operating business. The September balance sheet already contains the disposal proceeds, so they cannot also be added to equity value. Our base and bear cases are worth the asset floor, not the discounted cash flow; even the bull case leaves the shares far above our target.
thesis: The swing to profit is not operating leverage: other income of 24.6 IDR bn carried the nine months while the operating line was a loss and the exit-quarter gross margin was under one per cent.

Poultry economics are hostile and AYAM is a price-taker: farm-gate live birds trade below independent producers' cost of production, and the company sells feed-cost-exposed product into a domestic market it does not set.

The discounted cash flow has no value to give: even with the terminal year normalised to a mid-cycle margin and struck at replacement capital spending, the enterprise value does not clear the net debt, so the equity value is the asset floor.

The asset floor is real - book equity of 226 IDR bn against a market capitalisation of IDR1,992.0bn - but it is worth a fraction of the price at the peer multiple, and the base and bear cases both sit on it.
The bull case is government supply discipline lifting live-bird prices while the chick line compounds, and even that case leaves the shares far above our target.

blocks.text: **Revision note - the corrected interim report for the nine months to September 2026 [S10].** We maintain PT Janu Putra Sejahtera at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp19**, a return of -96.2% from the Rp498 close [S0]. The target is modestly below the one this desk published on 6 November, and the rating is unchanged. The move is not a change of view about poultry prices: it is the net of two corrections to our own model and a move of the valuation date. First, the other income line was carried in earnings as though it were a normal run-rate while the same value was also credited through the associate's book value in the investments line, and it was excluded from free cash flow; the line is now carried at the filed actual for the current year and at zero thereafter, with the reasons set out in the financial section [S10, F52; S6, F66-F68]. Second, FY2027E gross margin was cut a point below FY2026E although the linked corn and soymeal curves do not move between the two years; it is now held at the same input, so the base case no longer contains an unsourced margin squeeze. Third, the valuation date has moved from 30 June to 30 September 2026, which is a date change and not an error correction: the 70.0 IDR bn consideration is no longer a bridge item because the proceeds now sit inside the September cash, the fixed assets bought with them and the debt repaid - 55.8 IDR bn received on the disposal, 20.8 IDR bn paid for new fixed assets, 35.1 IDR bn of net investing inflow, 6.2 IDR bn of net increase in cash and 8.3 IDR bn of cash left at the period end [S10, F56-F63, F61] - and only the part that stayed in cash or repaid debt reduced net debt, while the part spent on new capacity re-entered property, plant and equipment. What the quarter itself says is unchanged: pre-tax profit of 19.2 IDR bn rests on other income of 24.6 IDR bn - more than twice the gross profit of 10.6 IDR bn - on tax of 1.6 IDR bn and net profit of 17.6 IDR bn, and the gross margin of the September quarter itself is under one per cent [S10, S3, S0].

The sections that follow carry the analysis in full and repeat the argument here only as far as the new accounts change it. The company is a small integrated poultry producer - parent-stock breeding, day-old chicks, commercial broilers, table eggs and a slaughterhouse - selling only into the domestic market [S6]. The shares have re-rated violently: the market capitalisation is IDR1,992.0bn, more than eight times the September book value of 226 IDR bn, and the stock trades at many times the book value of a business whose return on that book has been close to nothing [S0].

The variant view is simple, and it is not a cautious one. The market is paying for a turnaround that has happened in the headline and has not happened in the business. The nine months to September produced a net profit of 17.6 IDR bn on sales of 203 IDR bn, but other income of 24.6 IDR bn - a line the interim accounts do not decompose, against 10.6 IDR bn of gross profit [S10, F19, F20, F21, F52] - was larger than the entire gross profit. Strip it out and the operating result was close to breakeven on a nine-month average that a single strong first quarter flatters: the second quarter earned about one per cent and the third under one per cent [S0]. The industry the company sells into has farm-gate live birds at 17,000 IDR per kg per kilogram against an independent producer's cost of production of 22,500 IDR per kg, a loss per kilogram that has persisted for weeks [S7].

What moves the value is therefore not demand. It is three things. First, whether live-bird and chick prices recover above cost, which is a policy question as much as a market one [S9]. Second, what rent the company now pays for the farms it no longer owns, because the lease was signed the same day the assets were transferred and the terms are not in the public disclosure [S8]. Third, whether the capacity the company has just spent 20.8 IDR bn building earns a return rather than adding to an already oversupplied market - the corrected interim shows the money has gone out, and nothing in the material we hold shows what it bought or what it will earn [S10, F57, S6]. Our base case is a cycle that recovers from the trough to 5.0% by FY2030E - below every year the company earned before the downturn - and on that path the equity is worth Rp15 a share.

We are deliberately not taking the most cautious path, and the way we avoid it is by anchoring on what the company actually reported. The nine months produced gross profit of 10.6 IDR bn on sales of 203 IDR bn, a margin of about five per cent [S3, F19, F20], and we carry the fourth quarter at the rate just reported rather than at that nine-month average, so the full year realises 4.2% with the December quarter at about one per cent. The second and third quarters were a trough at about one per cent [S0], and we do not extrapolate the trough any more than we extrapolate the first quarter. The chick business is genuinely growing and the cost of sales fell faster than sales, which is why the base case returns to the mid-cycle margin by FY2030E instead of staying at the run-rate. Even so, the value that produces against a price of Rp498 is the whole of the call: the operating improvement is real but small, and the price already assumes a franchise the company has not built.

One consequence of the corrected model has to be stated plainly, because it is the call. The discounted cash flow supports an enterprise value of IDR-7.6bn - negative, because at replacement capital spending the present value of the explicit-period cash outflow outweighs a positive but modest terminal value - against net debt the September balance sheet carries once the current maturities of the bank loans are added back [S10, F58, F59, F60, F61]. The equity value from the cash flow is therefore nil before any cross-check, and its unfloored equity value is negative - the enterprise value less net debt plus the investments line - so the engine floors it at nil before it reaches the blend. What puts a floor under the shares is not the operating business but the balance sheet: at 226 IDR bn of book equity, the peer-median price-to-book of the three covered integrated producers implies Rp46 a share, and P/BV carries thirty per cent of the blend [S0, S3, F24]. The base case is worth Rp15 and so is the bear; the bull is worth Rp28. The twelve-month target of Rp19 is the probability-weighted value of the three scenarios, and because the base and the bear both sit on the asset floor, the mode of the distribution is that floor and the target is above it only by the bull branch weighted at a quarter - the probability we defend in the risks section. That is not caution dressed as arithmetic. It is what a low single-digit gross margin, an operating cost base at the witnessed rate, a rent obligation and a capital structure that does not clear its own debt do to the discounted cash flow, and it is why the asset value, not the cash flow, is the only thing holding up the equity. The sensitivity table shows the same thing from the other side: a point of gross margin moves the discounted cash flow by more than the whole value it produces.

Poultry in Indonesia is a commodity business with a long history of boom and bust. Breeders and
integrators make money when the national flock is short and lose it when everyone expands at once.
The product is perishable, the price is set daily at the farm gate, and the smallest producers carry
the least bargaining power with feed suppliers and buyers. A company without its own feed mill buys
the most expensive part of its cost base at retail and sells its output at wholesale. That is the
structural position here, and it is why we weight operating economics far above headline earnings
and why a re-rating of the shares does not, by itself, change what the business is worth.

AYAM is a vertically integrated poultry producer built around four revenue lines: commercial broiler sales from its own farms, day-old chicks from parent-stock breeding and hatchery operations, table eggs from layer farms, and chicken carcasses plus tolling services through its slaughterhouse [S6]. The company describes its purpose as poultry farming, poultry slaughtering and packing, and livestock supporting services, and it serves the domestic market only [S6]. It listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in November 2023 and had 4,000 m shares shares outstanding at the end of FY2025 [S6, F38]. It employed 311 people people at that date, down from the prior year as the cost programme ran through the organisation [S6, F39].

The revenue mix has inverted, and that is the single most important operating fact about the company. In FY2025 commercial broiler sales were 136 IDR bn, day-old chicks 107 IDR bn, eggs 23.6 IDR bn and carcasses and tolling 0.8 IDR bn [S6, F25-F28]. A year earlier the broiler line was more than twice the chick line; by FY2025 the two had almost crossed, and by the nine months of 2026 the chick line was 144 IDR bn of revenue after growing by more than four-fifths year on year [S3, F23]. The broiler business, which was the core of the company at listing, has shrunk to a minority of sales. That growth is the single factual support for our bull case: the product is priced at 8,800 IDR per bird a bird, above the level at which the downstream flock still buys [S7, F34], and the volume is running into a policy that culls parent stock at fifty to fifty-five weeks against a laying life of 65.0 weeks [S9, F41].

The economics of that shift are different in kind. A broiler is a commodity sold by weight into a market where the farm-gate price is set by supply and demand and where independent producers currently lose money on every kilogram [S7, F29, F30]. A day-old chick is a breeder product sold to other farmers who intend to raise it; its price tracks the cost of the parent-stock operation and the appetite of the downstream flock, and its volume is directly exposed to government supply management, which culls productive parent stock early to control the number of chicks reaching the market [S9, F41]. Being a chick seller therefore means holding a policy-sensitive volume and a cost-linked price, which is a better position than being a live-bird seller but not a moat.

The production chain runs from parent-stock farms, through a hatchery, into broiler and layer farms, and out through a slaughterhouse that also takes tolling work [S6]. The company also holds a fifth of an associate, PT Janu Putra Abadi [S6, F40], whose profit share arrives in other income rather than in the operating line, and whose contribution has been volatile.

The ownership of that chain changed materially in the middle of 2026. On 29 July the company transferred fifteen land plots totalling 129,645 sqm square metres, the buildings standing on them, and the plant and equipment that supports operations, to PT Universal Agri Bisnisindo for 70.0 IDR bn, equal to 33.5% of FY2025 equity, and signed a lease agreement over the same assets on the same day so that it keeps using them [S8, F35-F37]. The company presents the transaction as providing flexibility in asset and funding management. The economic substance is a sale and leaseback: the company has converted owned capacity into a consideration and a rent obligation, which lowers depreciation and raises operating cost, and which fixes a claim on its cash flow ahead of shareholders. The disclosure states the consideration but not how it was settled - cash or an offset - nor the rent, so both are analysed from the balance sheet rather than assumed [S8]. Two gaps in it are unresolved. The counterparty, PT Universal Agri Bisnisindo, does not appear in the FY2025 related-party note, which names only PT Janu Putra Abadi and CV Jaya Medika [S6], but the disclosure does not state that it is a third party either, so we treat the relationship as unverified. And the 70.0 IDR bn consideration does not reconcile to the 55.8 IDR bn of cash the interim cash-flow statement shows received on disposal, with the difference unexplained; we add no bridge item for it because no receivable is disclosed [S10, F35, F56, S8].

Strategically the company is a challenger in every sense. It is a single-province producer selling into a domestic market with no consumer brand and no export channel, and a balance sheet that has been financed by supplier credit and bank debt rather than by equity [S0, S6]. We find no disclosure of feed milling of its own in the material we hold, and its own cost discussion is about the price of purchased feed inputs rather than a milling margin [S6, S7]; the cost-link shares in our model are our own estimates for that reason. Its scale is a fraction of the integrated groups it competes with. The investment case does not rest on it becoming an integrator; it rests on whether a small breeder can earn a return in a market that is oversupplied and administratively managed.

The national poultry complex is in oversupply, and the price evidence is unambiguous. Independent producers report farm-gate live-bird prices of 17,000 IDR per kg per kilogram against a cost of production of 22,500 IDR per kg, a loss of several thousand rupiah on every kilogram sold, and they say the condition has persisted for almost three weeks [S7, F29, F30]. The cost stack behind that number is feed at 10,000 IDR per kg per kilogram, feed-grade corn at 7,800 IDR per kg, imported soybean meal at 10,000 IDR per kg, and day-old chicks above 8,800 IDR per bird a bird [S7, F31-F34]. Producers are asking government to cut the cost of raw materials, to enforce the reference purchase price against slaughterhouses and brokers, and to direct integrator volume away from traditional markets [S7].

Policy is the swing factor in this industry, not the weather and not the consumer. The breeders' association, of which AYAM is a member [S6], describes a system in which government manages chick supply by culling productive parent stock early - at fifty to fifty-five weeks against a normal laying life of 65.0 weeks - and in which producers are told not to price too high during the festive season nor too low afterwards [S9, F41]. A corn support programme runs alongside it [S9]. The association's concern is that supply control sits awkwardly with competition law, which is why it is arguing for the rules to be synchronised as the competition statute is revised [S9]. For a chick seller, that is a policy-set volume. For a live-bird seller, it is a policy-influenced price. Neither is a market the company controls.

Our sector deck prices the two inputs that dominate cost, corn and soybean meal, and both are forecast above spot. That matters more here than in most consumer names because the margin is single-digit: a feed-cost rise of the size the deck carries is most of the profit, and the company has no pricing power to offset it. The evidence for that absence of pricing power is in the company's own segment disclosure, where broiler revenue collapsed while chick revenue grew [S6, F25, F26]. That is what a price-taker's mix looks like when it chases the one product that still has demand.

The mapping from the deck to this company's cost base needs to be stated, because the levels are far apart and the report should not leave the reader to guess. The deck's corn curve is a world price in US dollars a tonne, and at the macro deck's rupiah rate it converts to a level well below the domestic feed-grade corn of 7,800 IDR per kg per kilogram that the producers' survey reports [S7, F32]; the gap is the corn support programme and domestic logistics [S9]. We do not use the deck as a price level. The cost links in the model take only the ratio of each forecast year to the FY2025 base year and apply it to the corn- and soymeal-exposed share of cost of sales, so the domestic level is already inside the witnessed gross margin and the world curve supplies the direction of travel only [S6, S7]. That transmission is imperfect, because an administered price can hold below the world market for a season, which is why the exposed share is set at a third of cost of sales rather than at the full feed weight and only part of a move passes into prices.

Competitive positioning is weak and we do not dress it up. Market share is not disclosed by the company and no industry body publishes a share for a producer of this size, so we cannot size it against the national flock [S6]. On the five forces: supplier power is high, because feed and corn are concentrated and policy-priced; buyer power is high, because integrators, traders and slaughterhouses set the farm-gate price; the threat of entry is high at the smallholder end where capital requirements are modest; substitutes are weak in the abstract but irrelevant at these margins; and rivalry is severe because the product is undifferentiated and perishable. The only candidate moat is breeding stock and hatchery capacity, and it is not exclusive: the association's own membership is a list of breeders [S9].

External influences run through three channels. The first is the rupiah, because soybean meal is imported and priced in dollars; the macro deck's exchange-rate path feeds straight into the cost link in our model [S0]. The second is agricultural policy on corn, which determines whether feed cost tracks the world market or a domestic administered price [S9]. The third is the supply management regime itself, which can lift prices by culling or crush them by allowing expansion [S9, F41]. None of these is within the company's control, and all three dominate its margin.

The five-year record is a business that shrank and then stabilised at a much lower level of profitability. Revenue was IDR395.6bn in FY2022, IDR352.3bn in FY2023, IDR361.3bn in FY2024 and IDR267.1bn in FY2025 [S0, S6]. Cost of sales took IDR258.2bn of the latest year, leaving gross profit of IDR8.9bn, a gross margin of 3.3% against 5.7% a year earlier [S6]. Operating expenses of IDR12.9bn then produced an operating loss of IDR-4.0bn [S6, F7], and the year reached net profit of only IDR0.1bn because other income and the associate's share covered the shortfall [S6, F15]. The FY2025 result is, in substance, a nil year.

Two data-pack lines are wrong and we restate both. Depreciation charged in FY2025 was IDR6.0bn - depreciation in cost of sales plus depreciation in general and administrative expense - and not the fraction the pack carries, because the cash-flow statement is prepared on the direct method and has no depreciation add-back line [S6, F9]. The FY2024 charge was IDR7.5bn [S6, F10]. We also restate the operating result to the figure the income statement reports, which differs from the pack in both years [S6, F7, F8]. The effect is to lift FY2025 EBITDA to IDR1.9bn and to make the cash cost of production visible rather than flattered: at the pack's depreciation the business looks as though it barely uses capital, which is the opposite of the truth for a breeder with farms, cages and hatcheries.

Cash generation is thin. Operating cash flow was -26.4 IDR bn in FY2024, because working capital absorbed cash as inventory and receivables built, and recovered to 4.7 IDR bn in FY2025 as the company ran the balance sheet down [S6, F13, F14]. Capex was IDR1.7bn in FY2025 [S6, F11] - a business that had stopped investing because it could not earn a return on new capacity - and then 20.8 IDR bn in the nine months to September 2026, funded by the farm sale [S10, F57]. That is the single largest change in the accounts this quarter and it cuts both ways: it is the first real investment the company has made in years, and it is cash that has left the business with no disclosed project, capacity or return attached to it. We carry it in the current year and do not extrapolate it (the valuation section says what happens if it continues). Working capital is trade-financed, with inventory and payables of similar magnitude against a modest revenue base, and the company relies on supplier credit rather than equity to fund the flock; the nine months show that credit being paid down, with payments to suppliers running ahead of receipts from customers [S0, S10].

The balance sheet carries the risk. Net debt was IDR40.2bn at the FY2025 year-end [S0], against an equity base of IDR208.8bn at the same date [S0], and at 30 September 2026 the company carried cash of 8.3 IDR bn against short-term bank loans of 23.9 IDR bn, current maturities of long-term bank loans of 4.9 IDR bn and non-current bank loans of 9.8 IDR bn [S10, F58-F61]. Finance expenses of IDR4.4bn in FY2025 consumed more than the whole operating result [S6, F17], though the nine months of 2026 charged 3.0 IDR bn as the debt was repaid [S10, F53]. A company with a gross margin in the low single digits and an interest bill of that size has almost no room to absorb a bad year, which is why the sale and leaseback was necessary and why it is not costless.

The nine-month actual changes the shape of the current year without changing its quality. Sales of 203 IDR bn were down on the prior year, but cost of sales fell faster, and gross profit of 10.6 IDR bn replaced a gross loss [S10, S3, F20, F42]. Then other income of 24.6 IDR bn - which the interim notes do not decompose - carried pre-tax profit of 19.2 IDR bn to a level the operating business did not earn; the operating line itself was a loss, because selling expenses of 2.4 IDR bn and general and administrative expenses of 9.0 IDR bn together exceed the gross profit [S10, F49-F55]. Tax of 1.6 IDR bn leaves net profit of 17.6 IDR bn, and equity of 226 IDR bn at the end of September is the number the market is looking at; the operating line underneath it is the number that matters [S10, S3]. The cash-flow statement does not reconcile the 70.0 IDR bn consideration to the 55.8 IDR bn received, and no separately disclosed disposal gain appears in the interim material we hold; we therefore neither capitalise that line nor treat it as recurring [S10, F35, F52, F56].

Our forecast reflects that split. Revenue is IDR278.3bn this year, IDR300.5bn next year and IDR357.9bn by the end of the explicit period, growing at the rates in the assumption table [S3]. The realised gross margin is not held at the nine-month average, which a single strong first quarter flatters: it is 4.2% this year - the actual nine months plus a fourth quarter at the rate the third quarter just reported - 4.2% next year, held there because the FY2027E input is set at the same benchmark cost set as FY2026E and the deck's corn and soymeal curves are flat between the two years, and then a recovery to 5.0% by FY2030E as the cycle normalises to a level below every year the company earned before the downturn [S0, S3]. From FY2031E the realised margin rises from 5.5% to 6.0% by FY2035E, a mid-cycle convergence below the 7.5%, 6.8% and 5.7% the company realised in FY2022-FY2024, because the deck's corn and soymeal curves escalate while only part of the cost passes into selling prices; the input margin rises with them so the terminal year is a normalised operating level rather than a trough. Other non-operating income is IDR23.0bn this year - the 24.6 IDR bn booked in the nine months net of the other expenses the interim P&L also carries - and nil thereafter [S10, F52, F54]. We do not extrapolate it, and the reason matters for the target. The line has run at 4.1 IDR bn in FY2025, 3.5 IDR bn in FY2024 and 6.2 IDR bn in FY2023 [S6, F66-F68], so it is volatile rather than a run-rate; the interim accounts do not decompose it, so the one-off part cannot be separated from the durable part [S10, F52]; the only component we can identify is the associate's equity-method share - a fifth-owned stake [S6, F40] that the valuation carries at book in the investments line - and capitalising its profit share in the cash flow as well would count the same asset twice. Carrying the line in earnings while excluding it from free cash flow would flatter earnings per share without adding value, so it stops at the filed actual. Operating cost is set at the witnessed rate: IDR15.2bn this year, the nine months of selling and administrative expense plus a fourth quarter at the nine-month run-rate, and then held in real terms plus the full-year rent the two months in the nine-month accounts do not carry, so the ratio eases only slowly as revenue grows to FY2030E [S10, F50, F51, S8]. That is about a percentage point of revenue above the input the previous version carried, and at this company's margins it is most of the operating result. Capital spending is IDR21.7bn this year, the amounts actually paid, and then back to the witnessed rate: the build is funded, nothing in the material we hold discloses what it is for, and carrying it forward would assume a programme nobody has described [S10, F57, S6, F11].

Two mechanics of the forecast table need a word, because they look like errors and are not. FY2026E net profit of IDR11.7bn is below the 17.6 IDR bn the nine months already earned, because the engine taxes the full year at the statutory rate while the reported nine months carried 1.6 IDR bn on pre-tax profit of 19.2 IDR bn [S10, F54, F55]. And FY2026E cash runs slightly negative because the forecast funds the year's capital spending from the FY2025 opening balance and holds debt flat; the balance sheet the valuation uses is the actual 30 September one, which carries 8.3 IDR bn of cash [S10, F61]. Neither affects free cash flow to the firm, which is struck before interest and does not use the cash line.

The funding plan for the negative free cash flow years has to be stated, because the model holds debt and the share count flat and neither is a plan the company has filed. FY2026E free cash flow to the firm is negative mainly because the 20.8 IDR bn of capital spending has already been paid, and it was paid out of the disposal proceeds inside the nine months, so the year's funding is done [S10, F56, F57]. The forecast hole is FY2027E and FY2028E: free cash flow to the firm of IDR-2.3bn and IDR-3.0bn against 8.3 IDR bn of cash at 30 September [S10, F61]. That is covered by cash if the bank lines are rolled. They are the constraint: short-term bank loans of 23.9 IDR bn and current maturities of 4.9 IDR bn fall due within twelve months against a current ratio below one [S10, F58, F59, S0], and the nine months show 3.0 IDR bn of finance cost being paid while debt was retired [S10, F53], which tells us the banks have been repaid rather than that they have committed to renew. The base case assumes they renew; if they do not, a rights issue or a discounted private placement is the modal outcome on this exchange, and the risks section prices that dilution as a downside rather than bury it in the cash flow [S0].

Earnings quality is the central analytical issue and we run the method card on it explicitly. The accruals pattern is adverse: profit has repeatedly run ahead of operating cash, and the current year's headline profit is dominated by a non-operating line the accounts do not decompose rather than by operations [S3, S6, S10, F52]. Inventory has outgrown cost of sales as the flock and feed stocks were carried through the downturn, and working capital is financed by supplier credit [S0]. None of this is manipulation-class: the disclosure is clear, the asset transfer was announced, and the auditor issued a clean opinion [S6, S8]. It is optics-class in the precise sense the card defines - headline earnings overstate the earning power of the business - and our valuation neither capitalises other income nor assumes it recurs.

We use a discounted cash flow as the primary method because the value of this company is the cash its assets produce, and we pair it with one asset cross-check because the cash flow itself cannot carry the equity: the earnings base earned nothing in the last audited year and the enterprise value does not clear the debt, so the residual claim is worth what the balance sheet is worth, not what a trough year's earnings will bear [S0, S6]. The asset cross-check is P/BV on book equity of 226 IDR bn at the median multiple of the three covered integrated producers, CPIN, CPRO and JPFA, which is the peer group this report cites elsewhere [S0, S3]. The EV/EBITDA cross-check is retained at a fifth weight and lands at the floor. It stays while the P/E goes because the two floors are not the same object: trough EBITDA is a positive number that an acquirer would price, so the method returns a real, if negative, equity value that the engine floors; the P/E's denominator is a rounding-level net profit, so the multiple is undefined and its "value" is an artefact of a nil earnings base. We therefore keep the multiple that prices the operating business and drop the one that divides by nothing, rather than letting both push the target down. The cost of equity is built from a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium, a country risk premium for Indonesia and an industry beta of 90.0% unlevered, levered to 91.2% for the company's gearing [S0]. The result is a cost of equity of 11.9% and, after the debt weight and the after-tax cost of debt, a weighted average cost of capital of 11.9%, inside the house band for rupiah names [S0]. Terminal growth is 4.0%, below long-run nominal GDP for the country, which is the discipline the compounder card requires of a domestic-only producer [S0].

The explicit forecast and the terminal value together produce an enterprise value of IDR-7.6bn [S0]. The bridge from that to equity is where this company is misread, so we set it out line by line. The valuation starts from the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, which is the latest the company has filed [S10]: cash of 8.3 IDR bn against short-term bank loans of 23.9 IDR bn, current maturities of long-term bank loans of 4.9 IDR bn and non-current bank loans of 9.8 IDR bn [S10, F58-F61]. The data pack's debt line carries the first and third of those but not the current maturities, so the bridge deducts the omitted 4.9 IDR bn as a single item rather than leaving it out, and adds the associate stake already in the pack's investments line [S10, F59]. That is the whole bridge. The 29 July 2026 transfer of land, buildings and plant to PT Universal Agri Bisnisindo for 70.0 IDR bn, leased back the same day [S8, F35, F37], is not a bridge item, and the difference from the previous publication is a change of valuation date, not the correction of an error. That note valued the shares from the 30 June 2026 balance sheet, before the transfer, and carried the consideration as a separate item; this one starts from 30 September 2026, after it. The cash-flow statement shows what happened to the money inside the period: 55.8 IDR bn received on the disposal, 20.8 IDR bn paid for new fixed assets, 35.1 IDR bn of net investing inflow and 6.2 IDR bn of net increase in cash, after debt repayment, with 8.3 IDR bn left at the end [S10, F56-F63, F61]. Only the part of the proceeds that stayed in cash or repaid debt reduced net debt; the part spent on new capacity re-entered property, plant and equipment, and that is why the target moved by more than the bridge item removed. The September balance sheet confirms the movement: total assets of 496 IDR bn against 510 IDR bn at the prior year-end, total liabilities of 270 IDR bn against 302 IDR bn, and equity of 226 IDR bn against 209 IDR bn [S10, S3, F44-F48]. The consideration does not reconcile to the cash received and we add nothing for the gap [S10, F35, F56]. On that basis the discounted cash flow's equity value is negative even before the engine floors it - the enterprise value is negative and the net debt is a further deduction, only partly offset by the investments line - so the published DCF value per share is Rp0, and the blended value is Rp15 a share, struck as 50% on the floored cash flow, 30% on the P/BV cross-check and 20% on EV/EBITDA [S0]. The enterprise value is negative because the explicit forecast consumes more cash in present value than the positive terminal value returns, which the next paragraph explains: the cash flow is small because the margin is small, operating cost sits at the witnessed rate, and the rent runs through operating cost [S6, S8, S10].

The terminal value is the number that decides this valuation, so we strike it honestly and report the consequence. In the last two actual years capital spending ran far below depreciation - IDR1.7bn against IDR6.0bn of depreciation [S6, F11, F9] - and capitalising that gap in perpetuity would value an indefinite run-off of the asset base. Terminal capital spending is therefore set equal to the long-run depreciation rate, so the perpetuity replaces the assets it consumes, and the terminal margin is normalised: the input margin rises across the years after FY2030E so the realised margin converges to a mid-cycle 6.0% by FY2035E instead of sagging to the trough the earlier version carried; the financial section shows the path. On that basis the terminal year earns a positive operating profit and a positive free cash flow, and the terminal value is positive. The enterprise value is still negative, because the present value of the explicit-period cash outflow is larger than the positive terminal value, and the debt is a further deduction. The consequence is plain: the cash-flow method says the equity is worth nothing, and everything in our target comes from the asset cross-check in the next paragraph.

The asset cross-check is not a comfort blanket, and we size it as the floor rather than the value. P/BV at the peer median of 0.8 times implies Rp46 a share, and that is the number carrying the target [S0, S3, F24]. It is a generous floor for three reasons: those peers earn a return on book that AYAM does not, the multiple is applied to a book value whose own assets have just been sold at a gain and cannot be independently appraised from the disclosure, and it assumes the balance sheet is worth its stated equity after a sale and leaseback that transferred a third of that equity to an unverified counterparty [S8, F36]. A distressed producer with a nil return on equity and no dividend would normally trade at a discount to the peer median, not at it, which is why the weight on P/BV is thirty per cent rather than the whole of the target.

The cross-checks diverge, and the divergence is diagnostic rather than embarrassing. We drop the P/E from the blend altogether rather than carry it at a token weight. The engine strikes multiples on last-twelve-month earnings, those earnings are the nil FY2025 year - IDR0.1bn [S6, F15] - and a multiple applied to a year that earned nothing returns almost nothing and is floored at zero, so the method can only ever push the value down: that is a floor dressed as a cross-check, which is what the method card warns against. The EV/EBITDA cross-check is struck on the same trough year's EBITDA and, once net debt is deducted and the omitted current maturities added, it produces Rp0 a share against the discounted cash flow's Rp0 and P/BV's Rp46 [S0]. We explain that divergence rather than average it: the trough EBITDA and the cash flow both capitalise a business that does not cover its capital cost, while the asset cross-check capitalises the balance sheet, and the gap between them is the difference between what the business earns and what it owns. Both operating methods are at the floor, which is itself the statement: neither the trough multiple nor the cash flow puts value above the net debt, and the equity is worth its assets only because the assets are worth more than the debt.

The two assumptions carrying most of the value are the realised gross margin and the revenue path. A change of a percentage point in the gross margin moves the discounted cash flow by more than that method is worth in the blend, which tells you how little equity cushion sits above the debt: the enterprise value has to clear net debt before the shareholder receives anything, and the margin is the only lever large enough to do it [S0]. The target moves less than the cash flow because the asset cross-check, which does not depend on the margin, carries most of it: the grid is the operating sensitivity, not a range around the published target.

What the price implies is the cleanest statement of the mispricing. A reverse discounted cash flow at Rp498 does not bracket on any revenue growth we can justify, because the current capitalisation requires an enterprise value several times what the witnessed margin can service [S0, S3]. The market is not discounting this company's cash flows; it is pricing an option on a policy-driven recovery, and the option is expensive relative to the cash flow that would have to arrive to justify it.

One dating point, because it is the kind of small mechanical gap that compounds into a wrong answer. The target is the blended value per share rolled forward twelve months at the cost of equity from the 30 September 2026 valuation date the discounted cash flow discounts from, which is the house twelve-month convention [S10]. The price we quote is the latest close in the data pack, so the two dates do not coincide; rolling the target to the price date instead would add a few weeks of discounting, a small amount of value, and changes no conclusion. The per-share figures in this section are per-share values throughout, not equity totals.
The risks that matter, with our judgement of likelihood and impact:

items: **Poultry price cycle (high likelihood, high impact).** Farm-gate live birds trade below
independent producers' cost of production, and the condition has persisted for weeks [S7, F29,
F30]. The company cannot set its own selling price, so a prolonged trough passes straight through
to its margin.
**Feed cost (high, high).** Corn and soybean meal are forecast above spot in our sector deck, and
the cost links in our model pass only part of that through to selling prices [S7, F31-F33]. On a
single-digit gross margin, a feed move of the deck's size is most of the profit.
**Policy (medium, high).** Chick supply and parent-stock culling decisions are administrative
[S9, F41]. A change in the culling rule changes both the volume the company sells and the price it
gets, in the same direction at once.
**Lease and balance-sheet risk (medium, high).** After the sale and leaseback the company pays
rent on the assets it operates, out of a margin that barely covers it, and net debt is large
relative to cash flow [S8, F35-F37]. The lease terms are not disclosed in the material we hold, so
the rent is a range, not a number. The base and the bear both charge the annualised rent implied by
the nine-month accounts - the two months booked since 29 July grossed up to a year, which is why
operating cost is held at IDR17.3bn rather than at the nine-month run-rate alone
[S10, F50, F51, F9]. The upper end of the range is a market yield on the 70.0 IDR bn
consideration, which would be a multiple of the depreciation the sale removed and would take the
operating line below zero on its own [S10, S8, F9]. We do not charge the upper end in the bear as
well as the base, because we cannot source it and a one-sided shock would hand the bull a rent
reduction nobody has disclosed; the value at the upper end is lower than the base on any cash-flow
measure and the same on the asset cross-check, so the target does not move by more than a rounding
step between the two ends.
**Liquidity and dilution (medium, high).** The free float is 23.5% and insiders hold
79.0% [S0], so the register is concentrated enough for the controlling
interest to determine a vote, and the three-month average daily traded value of
IDR13.5bn is small against a market capitalisation of
IDR1,992.0bn. At 30 September 2026 cash of 8.3 IDR bn stood against
23.9 IDR bn of short-term bank loans, 4.9 IDR bn of current maturities and 9.8 IDR bn of
non-current bank loans [S10, F58-F61], and the current ratio is below one [S0], so the balance sheet is
not liquid without the banks renewing. Free cash flow to the firm is negative through FY2028E
[S0], and a rights issue or discounted private placement sized to close that gap is the modal IDX
outcome for a position like this: it would enlarge the share count at a price below book and cut
our per-share values roughly in proportion, which is the main way the asset floor itself could
break. The bear case charges two points more for the refinancing risk; the dilution is disclosed
here rather than modelled because no corporate action has been announced [S0].
**Governance (medium, medium).** An asset sale equal to a third of book equity to a counterparty
whose relationship to the company cannot be established, leased back the same day, whose pricing
and rent cannot be benchmarked from the disclosure we hold [S8, F35, F36, S6].
**Execution (medium, medium).** The chick line is growing quickly off a small base and now
dominates revenue [S3, F23]; a policy-driven slowdown in chick demand would hit the one line that
is working.

blocks.text: Bear (25.0%) values the shares at Rp15: oversupply persists into the next cycle, the gross margin stays at the exit run-rate instead of converging on the FY2025 witnessed level, revenue growth is three points lower, and refinancing costs two points more. Base (50.0%) is Rp15: the margin recovers from the trough to 5.0% by FY2030E and converges to a mid-cycle 6.0% by FY2035E, below the FY2022 and FY2023 realisations, and revenue grows modestly, but the operating cash flow still does not clear the net debt, so the equity is worth the asset floor and no more. Bull (25.0%) is Rp28: supply discipline lifts live-bird prices back above cost of production, the gross margin returns to the top of the range the company earned in FY2022 to FY2024 and above it at the peak, the chick line keeps compounding, and refinancing is cheaper.

The bear and the base produce the same per-share value, and that is a result rather than a mistake: both are floored by the asset cross-check, which does not depend on the cycle, and the difference between them sits in the forecast table as a lower EBITDA and a lower cash flow that the debt absorbs before it reaches the shareholder. The mode of the distribution is the asset floor, and the target sits above it only because the bull branch is weighted at a quarter. We defend that quarter rather than assert it. The bull rests on three things that have already happened: day-old-chick sales rose more than four-fifths to 144 IDR bn, now more than two-thirds of revenue [S3, F23]; the price of a chick is above the level at which the downstream flock still buys, 8,800 IDR per bird a bird [S7, F34]; and the sale and leaseback retired bank debt, taking net debt from IDR40.2bn at FY2025 to the September position [S0, S10, F58-F61]. On top of that sits a policy that culls parent stock at fifty to fifty-five weeks against a laying life of 65.0 weeks [S9, F41], which supports the price of the product AYAM sells. A quarter weight says those forces are real but not yet visible in the realised margin, and that the shares have already tripled in twelve months, so convergence to intrinsic value inside a twelve-month horizon is not something we would pay for. The bear and bull cases shock the same three drivers - revenue growth, gross margin and the cost of debt - by mirrored amounts, and the rent is not shocked on either side, so the asymmetry in the outcomes comes from the operating leverage in a business with a thin margin and from the asset floor beneath both, not from a stacked set of assumptions. Even the bull case does not reach today's price, which is the honest statement of the call: the shares are expensive in every scenario we can defend, they are simply less catastrophically expensive if supply discipline works.

Signposts that would change our view. First, two consecutive quarters of farm-gate prices above independent cost of production, which would tell us the culling regime is working [S7, F29, F30]. Second, audited accounts in which the operating line, not other income, carries the profit [S3]. Third, disclosure of the lease terms, which would let us size the rent claim properly [S8]. Fourth, evidence that the layer capacity is earning a return rather than adding to the national surplus [S6]. Any two of those together would justify revisiting the bear case; the first alone would justify revisiting the sector view, not the stock.

Control is concentrated. Insiders hold 79.0% of the shares and the free float is 23.5% [S0], so the controlling interest can determine the outcome of any shareholder vote. The board is led by a president commissioner and a president director, and the company maintains an audit committee, a nomination and remuneration committee, a corporate secretary, an internal audit unit and an internal control system, all described in the annual report [S6]. The auditor is Jonnardi, Jamaludin, Sukimto & Rekan, a member of Audittrust International, and the opinion on the FY2025 accounts is "fairly, in all material respects" - a clean opinion [S6].

The governance event of the year is the asset transfer. Fifteen land plots of 129,645 sqm square metres, with the buildings and plant on them, went to PT Universal Agri Bisnisindo for 70.0 IDR bn, or 33.5% of FY2025 equity, and the company signed a lease over the same assets the same day so that it could keep operating them [S8, F35-F37]. The disclosure explains the rationale as flexibility in asset and funding management and states that operations, legal position, finances and going concern are unaffected. We take the disclosure at face value and still flag three things: the transaction transfers a third of book equity to a counterparty that the FY2025 related-party note does not name but that the disclosure does not affirm is a third party either, so the relationship is unverified rather than arm's length [S6, S8]; the 70.0 IDR bn consideration does not reconcile to the 55.8 IDR bn of cash the interim accounts show received [S10, F35, F56]; and neither the sale price nor the rent is benchmarked against an independent valuation in the disclosure. That is the modal value-destruction channel on this exchange, and it is the first question the red team should press.

Related-party gravity more broadly: the company sells and buys within a group that includes an associate it owns a fifth of [S6, F40], and the associate's profit share has swung between a profit and a loss across the last two years [S6]. We have not found evidence of sales to or purchases from affiliates at scale in the material we hold, but we also cannot rule it out from the summary disclosures, and we say so rather than assert either way.

Dividends: none since listing, and none in our forecast [S0]. With a nil audited profit, a leveraged balance sheet and a capital programme, a distribution is not a realistic use of cash in the near term, and the absence of a dividend record is consistent with that.

On ESG, the material exposures are the ones that come with livestock: animal welfare and stocking density, biosecurity and disease control, antibiotic use in feed, water and waste management at scale, and the labour intensity of farm work in a business with 311 people employees [S6, F39]. The company reports certifications, publishes a sustainability report alongside its annual report, and describes community programmes [S6]. We have not found an enforcement action, a special notation or a suspension in the sources we hold, and we make no claim beyond that.

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter; each is tied to a disclosure we hold [S3, S7, S8, S9]. Between updates we watch a short list of variables, because the investment case turns on a handful of numbers.

The first is the farm-gate live-bird price against independent cost of production, from the producer surveys published through the financial press; the gap between those two numbers is the best single indicator of whether the industry is recovering [S7, F29, F30]. The second is the cost of feed: corn and soybean meal prices, and any change in the corn support programme, feed straight into the cost links in our model [S9, F32, F33]. The third is chick supply policy, since culling decisions change both the volume the company sells and the price it receives [S9, F41].

At the company level we watch three things. The quarterly split between operating profit and other income, which tells us whether the business or the balance sheet is producing the result [S3]. Lease payments and any further asset transfers, which tell us how much of the sale proceeds the company is paying back as rent [S8]. And the audited FY2026 accounts, which will separate the disposal gain from the operating year for the first time and give us a clean base for the next forecast [S3]. We will update the coverage when the full-year accounts are published, or earlier if the price of live birds moves decisively above cost.
